en: The Sutra of the Nine-Colored Deer Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a nine-colored deer; its fur was of nine different colors."
His horns were as white as snow; he constantly grazed on water and grass by the banks of the Ganges and was always a friend to a crow.
At that time, a drowning man came floating down the current in the river, rising and sinking, until he caught hold of a tree branch. Looking up and crying out to heaven, he said:
"O mountain spirits, tree spirits, and all you devas and nāga spirits, why do you not have compassion for me?"
Upon hearing the person's cry, the deer immediately ran to the water’s edge and said to the drowning man:
"Do not be afraid! You may mount my back and grasp my horns; I shall carry you out onto the shore."

The deer, utterly exhausted, lowered himself to the ground where the man had been submerged. He circumambulated the deer three times, bowed his head to it, and begged to become its slave, offering to serve it by gathering water and grass.
The deer said, "I have no need for you; let us each depart. If you wish to repay my kindness, do not say that I am here, for people covet my hide and antlers and will surely come to kill me."
Thereupon, the drowning man accepted the instruction and departed.
At that time, the king’s consort dreamed at night of a nine-colored deer; desiring its hide and antlers, she immediately feigned illness and refused to rise.
The King asked the lady, "Why do you not rise? The lady replied:

"Last night I dreamed of an extraordinary deer; its fur was of nine different colors and its antlers were white as snow. I thought of obtaining its hide to make a robe and its antlers to make a fly-whisk handle. Your Majesty should obtain it for me; if Your Majesty does not obtain it, I shall die."
The king said to his consort:
"Rise for a moment; what is there that I, as the sovereign of a kingdom, cannot obtain?
The king then immediately issued a proclamation throughout the land:

"If there is anyone who can capture the nine-colored deer, I shall share my kingdom with them to rule, and grant them a golden bowl filled with silver grain, and a silver bowl filled with golden grain."
Upon hearing the king’s heavy reward for the drowned man, a wicked thought arose in his mind:
"I said that by finding this deer I could attain wealth and status; but the deer is a mere beast—what does it matter whether it lives or dies?"
He then said to the person who had offered the reward:
"I know where the nine-colored deer is.
The person who had offered the reward then led him to the king's presence and said:
"This man knows where the nine-colored deer is located.
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly delighted and said:
"If you bring its hide and horns, I shall reward you with half the kingdom."
"Then, leprosy broke out on the face of the drowning man.
The drowning man said:
'Although this deer is but an animal, it possesses great majestic power; Your Majesty should lead many men and soldiers, and only then can it be captured.'"
The king immediately dispatched a large force of soldiers to the banks of the Ganges.
Perched upon a tree, the crow saw the king’s retinue approaching from afar; suspecting they intended to kill the deer, he called out to the deer, saying, "Arise at once!"
"The king has come to take you.
The deer continued to lie there fast asleep and did not wake; the crow spoke again:
"Friend, please arise!"
"The King is leading his army here.
Yet the deer still did not wake; so the crow descended from the tree, perched upon its head, and pecked at its ear: "Friend, arise!"
"The king's troops have surrounded you in several layers.
Startled, the deer looked around in all directions; finding no way to flee across the ground, it went straight toward the side of the king's chariot.
A bystander drew his bow, intending to shoot it, but the king said, "Do not shoot this deer!
This deer is no ordinary creature; perhaps it is a celestial deity!
The deer then spoke:
"Do not shoot and kill me; grant me a brief moment, for I have rendered service to the kingdom.
The king asked, "What service have you performed?"
"I once saved a man within the kingdom.
He then knelt down for a long time and asked the king again,
"Who said that I was here?"
The king said, "He is a man with a leper’s face standing by the chariot.
The deer raised its head and looked at this man; tears fell from its eyes as it could not restrain itself.
"Great King! This man was originally drowning in the water, drifting downstream; now and then he emerged or submerged until he caught hold of a tree, whereupon he looked up and cried out to heaven:
'O mountain spirits, tree spirits, and all the devas and nāga spirits, why do you not take pity on me?'"
"At that time, I did not begrudge this life; I threw myself into the water, carried this man out, and made a solemn vow never to speak of it.
A person who lacks integrity is no better than a piece of wood floating in the water."
Upon hearing the deer’s words, the king showed a look of shame and said,
"My subjects lack righteousness.
The king then immediately instructed his people three times:
"Alas! Alas! Having received his grace, how can you wish to kill him in return?"
The king immediately released the deer, allowing it to depart, and declared:
"Within my kingdom, if there is anyone who drives this deer away, you shall be executed along with your five kinsmen.
Thereupon, the king returned to his palace.
The deer returned to its former dwelling.

At that time, the many deer of the kingdom all came to rely upon it, forming herds of several thousand. They were never harmed again; they shared in the water and grass together, and did not trespass upon the people's vegetables or grain.

From then on, wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the people suffered no diseases. During that era of great peace, they lived out their natural lifespans before passing away.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"In the conduct of a Bodhisattva, even when dwelling among animals, one does not abandon compassion;
thus humans and beasts are both delivered. The lady at that time was Sundarī."
At that time, the crow was Ānanda;
the man who had fallen into the water was Devadatta;
and the deer at that time was my own self.
“Devadatta has been my enemy life after life;
Ānanda possesses a sincere resolve and shall attain the Way.
Thus did the Bodhisattva further practice the pāramitā of diligent austerity, exercising patience in this manner.
The Sutra on the Nine-Colored Deer Spoken by the Buddha.
